1. The animation shows inflation eroding a fixed payment. A "first price" check, labeled as a flat amount, is compared with US consumer prices (CPI-U) over Aug 2006 to Aug 2026. Actual prices rose 64.3%. Twenty annual raises of 2% would only have added up to 48.6%. The whole thing is marked "ILLUSTRATIVE."

2. A gray bar for the starting amount appears first. A blue bar for prices in Aug 2026 then rises above it, and a dotted line marks where 20 raises of 2% would have ended up. The blue bar ends above that line. In the last two frames, text appears saying consumer prices are a national average, not one retiree's own basket.

3. Prices grew faster over those 20 years than a steady 2% a year would have. A payment that stays flat, or that rises by a fixed 2%, would buy less than it did at the start. The caveats say this is US history, not a forecast, and that your own costs could differ from the average.

4. The animation doesn't state any advice. A viewer could infer that a payout that doesn't adjust for inflation loses buying power over a long retirement. For me, a 64-year-old comparing two annuity options, that would mean checking whether either option has inflation protection or annual increases. It would also mean not assuming a 2% raise is enough.

5. The advice is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the comparison and the caveats. It never mentions annuities, payout options, or what to do.
